# Returns: A Redesign Proposal

*Draft for discussion — not a mandate. Assumptions are illustrative placeholders; swap in your actuals and the logic should hold.*

---

## 0. A note before the detail

There's a temptation in these situations to read "28% return rate" as the problem statement. I'd gently push back on that. A 28% rate in a category where customers order two sizes to keep one isn't necessarily a defect — it may be the cost of the conversion rate you're already enjoying. Customer research is telling you something worth hearing.

Three reframes seem to explain most of the leakage better than the policy does:

1. **The decision about a returned unit is currently made *after* it arrives.** That's the expensive part. Everything downstream — the queue, the double-touch, the late markdown — descends from a disposition decision that happens too late and in the wrong place.
2. **The enemy is the calendar, not the customer.** A grade-A unit is worth ~92% of ASP on day two and ~55% on day forty. Nothing physically changed. You paid for time.
3. **Return cost currently sits in operations' P&L but is created in merchandising's.** Until the buyer who chose the SKU feels the return in their number, prevention will always be someone else's project.

If those three are right, the redesign is less about restricting behaviour and more about **collapsing decision latency and relocating accountability.** What follows assumes that reading. Push back where it doesn't fit what you're seeing.

---

## 1. Where the money actually goes

Worth decomposing before prescribing. A returned unit destroys value in six places, and my suspicion is that only two of them are currently visible in anyone's reporting.

| Leak | Illustrative per returned unit | Visible today? |
|---|---|---|
| Reverse freight (prepaid label, low density) | $4.20 | Usually yes |
| Touch labour (receive, inspect, grade, repack, restock) | $2.60 | Usually yes |
| Reverse overhead (space, systems, supervision, congestion drag on outbound) | $1.40 | Rarely |
| **Value decay** (markdown taken because of elapsed time, not condition) | **$9.80** | Almost never |
| Scrap / write-off | $6.30 (blended) | Partially |
| Sunk outbound fulfilment + payment processing | $8.50 | Recognised but treated as unavoidable |

**Working illustration** (please replace): 10M units shipped, ASP $60, COGS $30, outbound fulfilment $6.50.

- Returns: 2.8M units, $168M refunded
- Blended net recovery today: ~42% of original retail (~$25.20/unit)
- Contribution on a *kept* unit: +$21.50
- Contribution on a *returned* unit: −$21.50
- **Swing per return: ~$43. Annual drag: ~$60M.** On $600M gross, that's roughly ten points of margin sitting in the reverse flow.

Notice that value decay plus scrap — the two purely self-inflicted lines — are about **$16 of the $32.80 of controllable loss.** That's where I'd look first, because it requires no change to the customer promise at all.

*Question worth putting to the finance team: does anyone currently own the value-decay line? If the answer is no, that may explain a lot.*

---

## 2. Prevention — reduce the *reason*, not the *right*

The goal isn't a lower return rate. It's a lower rate of **avoidable, low-recovery** returns, with conversion and repeat-purchase held flat or better as an explicit guardrail. Some returns are profitable to encourage; the trick is knowing which.

### 2.1 Segment the reasons first

Free-text and single-dropdown reason codes are close to useless — customers pick the first plausible option. Suggest a guided, two-step taxonomy captured at RMA initiation, then *reconciled against physical grade* so you can measure how much customers under- or over-report:

| Reason cluster | Typical share | Owner | Preventable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fit / size | 35–45% (apparel) | Merch + PDP | Highly |
| Expectation gap (colour, material, scale) | 15–20% | Content | Highly |
| Damaged in transit | 6–10% | Packaging + carrier | Highly |
| Defective / quality | 8–12% | Vendor | Highly, via chargeback |
| Wrong item / short ship | 3–5% | Fulfilment | Fully |
| Bracketing (intentional multi-buy) | 10–15% | Nobody, currently | Partly — and possibly shouldn't be |
| Remorse / no longer needed | 8–12% | — | Low |
| Abuse / wardrobing / serial | 1–3% | Risk | Yes, quietly |

### 2.2 Interventions, roughly in order of payback

**Pre-purchase**
- **Size intelligence from your own return exhaust.** You already know that customers who returned SKU-A in M kept it in L. That's a recommendation engine sitting unused. Expect 15–25% reduction in size-driven returns on covered SKUs; coverage matters more than model sophistication.
- **PDP truthfulness audits on the worst 200 SKUs by return rate.** Measured dimensions, on-body scale reference, fabric behaviour, video. Cheap, unglamorous, reliably effective.
- **Bracketing made explicit rather than accidental.** If a customer has two sizes in the cart, you have a choice: block it (loses share — the research is right), ignore it (costs $43 per returned unit), or *serve it deliberately* — offer a size advisor, or a "try both, return the spare free at a drop-off point" flow that steers the reverse leg into your cheapest, fastest lane. The third option turns a cost into a controlled cost.
- **Review surfacing weighted toward fit signal**, not star rating.

**Post-purchase, pre-return** — this is the highest-yield and most neglected window.
- **Exchange-first RMA flow.** Default to size/colour exchange with instant dispatch and a small incentive; refund available but one click deeper. Typical conversion 20–35% of eligible intents. This preserves *revenue*, not just margin — materially better than any cost reduction.
- **Returnless refund ("keep it") on a computed threshold**, not a flat rule. Approve when `expected net recovery < reverse freight + touch cost + expected decay`. On low-ASP, high-freight, low-recovery items this is simply the dominant choice. Typically 8–15% of return volume qualifies; gate it with velocity limits per customer to keep abuse under ~0.5%.
- **Partial keep / repair-kit / missing-part dispatch** for cosmetic or incomplete-order cases. Often converts a $43 loss into a $4 cost.
- **Defect containment at source.** Vendor scorecards with a returns reserve withheld per PO, released on performance. This changes supplier behaviour faster than any inspection regime.
- **Packaging redesign for the worst transit-damage SKUs.** Damage rate is a design variable, not weather.

### 2.3 Guardrails so prevention doesn't become tightening in disguise

Every prevention change ships as an experiment with three co-primary metrics: **return rate, conversion, and 12-month repeat rate of the exposed cohort.** Any intervention that improves return rate while degrading repeat rate is a loss, and should be reversed regardless of how good the operations number looks. I'd make that a standing rule and hold the team to it publicly.

---

## 3. Triage and grading — decide before it moves

The manual inspection queue is a symptom. The queue exists because disposition is decided at the dock. Move the decision upstream and most of the queue disappears.

### 3.1 Predicted disposition at RMA initiation

At the moment the customer requests a return, you know: SKU, condition self-report, guided photos, reason code, customer history, days-since-delivery, current inventory position, season position, and secondary-market price. That is more than enough to predict a disposition class with useful accuracy.

The RMA then carries a **disposition code printed on the label / encoded in the QR**, which determines routing before the unit is collected.

| Grade | Definition | Target share | Route | Net recovery target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Sellable as-new, sealed/unworn | 40–48% | Cross-dock → nearest FC forward stock | 88–96% of ASP |
| **B** | Open-box, cosmetically imperfect | 20–25% | RPC → own certified/open-box storefront | 62–78% |
| **C** | Functional, needs refurb or parts | 12–18% | RPC refurb cell or specialist partner | 45–65% post-refurb |
| **D** | Harvest / component or bulk B2B | 8–12% | Direct to jobber / auction | 10–25% |
| **E** | Recycle / regulated disposal | ≤4% | Certified processor | ~0 to negative |

### 3.2 Trusted fast lane

Grade-A prediction on a low-risk SKU from a low-risk customer should **bypass physical inspection entirely** and go direct to forward stock, with statistical audit sampling (start at 15%, decay to 3–5% as false-positive rate proves out) rather than 100% inspection. Target **35% of all returns cross-docked with zero inspection touch** by month twelve.

This is the single biggest labour and latency lever available. It also feels uncomfortable, which is roughly the right signal — the discomfort is a proxy for how much money the current caution is costing.

### 3.3 The queue rule

No unit sits "awaiting decision." Ever. A disposition is assigned within 4 hours of dock scan, or the system auto-assigns the default for that SKU class. **WIP age distribution becomes a daily-reviewed metric**, and any unit older than 72 hours triggers automatic escalation down the channel waterfall. Ambiguity is fine at the edges; ambiguity in the middle of a decaying-asset queue is expensive.

**SLA targets:** dock-to-disposition ≤ 4h · dock-to-resale-live ≤ 48h for A/B · refund issued at first carrier scan, not at receipt (this is a customer-promise upgrade that costs almost nothing and buys goodwill for everything else).

---

## 4. Refurbishment and secondary channels

### 4.1 Refurb only where the arithmetic says so

A simple gate, applied per SKU-grade pair and recalculated weekly:

> **Refurbish if:** `(price at grade N+1 − price at grade N) > refurb cost × (1 + rework failure rate) + handling delay decay`

Four tiers, ascending cost:
1. **Clean / repack / reseal** — $1.20–2.50. Almost always positive. Highest-volume activity by far.
2. **Accessory or consumable replacement from a parts bank** built from grade-D harvest — $3–8. Often the best-return activity in the whole operation, because the input is free.
3. **Technical repair** — $12–40. In-house only for high-velocity categories; otherwise a specialist partner on a per-unit or revenue-share basis.
4. **Harvest** — recover components to feed tier 2, then recycle the shell.

Make/buy: I'd resist building technical rep

# Critique: "Returns: A Redesign Proposal"

## A. Disqualifying issue: the deliverable is roughly half-finished

The brief named six required elements. The draft covers three, partially:

| Requested | Status |
|---|---|
| Return prevention | Covered, reasonably well |
| Triage & grading | Covered, well |
| Refurbishment & secondary channels | Cuts off mid-sentence ("I'd resist building technical rep") |
| **Network design for reverse flows** | **Absent** |
| **Data feedback loop to merchandising** | **Absent** |
| **How success should be measured / quantified** | **Absent** |

This is not a formatting nit. Section 0 stakes the entire argument on three reframes, and the third — "return cost sits in operations' P&L but is created in merchandising's" — is never operationalized anywhere in the document. The author declares the root cause and then doesn't treat it. Similarly, "value decay is the biggest leak" is asserted, and the section that would fix it (fast reverse network, regional processing, cross-dock siting) is missing. The draft is strongest exactly where the client's existing team could probably have got to on its own, and silent where the hard work is.

There is also no investment case at all: no program cost, capex, headcount, systems spend, phasing, or payback. No 30/60/90. As written, no executive can approve or fund anything in it.

## B. Quantitative errors and unreconciled numbers

The financial section will not survive a CFO's first pass.

1. **The leak table double-counts.** "Value decay $9.80" and "Scrap $6.30" are *already inside* the stated 42% blended net recovery used to derive the −$21.50 contribution. Summing the column ($32.80) and then separately citing a $43 swing gives the reader two incompatible loss figures with no bridge between them.
2. **"Controllable loss" is mislabelled.** The $32.80 total includes $8.50 of sunk outbound and payment processing, which the same table's own column describes as "unavoidable." You cannot call it controllable in the next paragraph.
3. **The annual drag figure is ambiguous to the point of misleading.** The reader is handed "$43 per return" and then "$60M annual drag." 2.8M × $43 = $120M. The $60M actually derives from 2.8M × $21.50. Both may be defensible measures (loss vs. swing-vs-kept), but presenting them adjacently without labelling invites either an overstatement of 2× or an accusation of one.
4. **"Ten points of margin" uses the wrong denominator.** $600M is gross shipped value; revenue after 28% returns is ~$432M. The drag is ~13.9% of recognised revenue, not 10%. Understating your own case on a base that was never booked is an avoidable error.
5. **The grade-mix table doesn't sum to 100%.** Range midpoints and endpoints permit 80%–107%. Sloppy in a table whose whole purpose is disposition allocation.
6. **The single most important number in the document is never calculated.** Applying the stated per-grade recovery targets to the stated mix implies a blended recovery of ~66% of ASP against today's 42% — roughly **$40M of annual recovery uplift**, before any prevention benefit. That is the headline of the proposal and it is left for the reader to compute. Nor is 66% stress-tested or sensitivity-ranged.
7. **The refurb gate formula is technically wrong.** `refurb cost × (1 + rework failure rate)` understates the economics of failure: a failed rework consumes the refurb cost *and* forfeits the pre-refurb salvage value. Correct form is expected-value: `uplift × P(success) > refurb cost + P(fail) × (value destroyed) + decay cost of the delay`.
8. **Unsourced effect sizes.** "15–25% reduction in size-driven returns," "20–35% exchange conversion," "8–15% qualify for returnless" are presented as engineering constants. Label them as benchmark ranges with a source and a pilot-derived confirmation step, or they will be treated as invented — which will contaminate the credible parts of the analysis.

Credit where due: the reverse-cost stack ($8.20) is internally consistent with the client's stated premise that returns cost more than the $6.50 outbound. That's a good catch. But $1.40 for "congestion drag on outbound" is implausibly small for an operation described as having goods *piling up* in a queue, and $2.60 of touch labour implies ~5 minutes fully loaded for receive-inspect-grade-repack-restock. Both look tuned to make the arithmetic land.

## C. The central analytical failure: the category is never resolved

The document simultaneously describes two different businesses and prescribes for both:

- Fit/size at 35–45%, PDP on-body scale, size advisors, wardrobing → **apparel**
- "Sealed/unworn," open-box storefront, technical repair at $12–40, parts banks, grade-D component harvest → **electronics/hardgoods**

These have almost nothing in common operationally. Apparel has near-zero refurb value, brutal season decay, and cross-dock-to-forward-stock is easy. Hardgoods have real refurb economics, data-wipe and battery/regulatory obligations, and much heavier reverse freight. Half of Section 4 is irrelevant to an apparel retailer and half of Section 2 is irrelevant to a hardgoods one. The draft should either declare the category assumption up front or branch the recommendation explicitly by category archetype and mix-weight the numbers. As written, the client cannot tell which half applies to them.

## D. Risk and compliance blind spots

1. **Refund at first carrier scan** is offered as a "costs almost nothing" goodwill upgrade. It is a well-known fraud vector (empty box, substituted item, brick-in-box). It needs a value ceiling, a customer-risk gate, an exception-handling and clawback process, and a quantified expected fraud cost. Presenting it as free is the least rigorous line in the document.
2. **Returnless refunds** carry unaddressed sales-tax/VAT reversal treatment, accounting/inventory write-off mechanics, and a disclosure dilemma: publish the rule and it is gamed; hide it and you invite "why did she get to keep it" fairness complaints. The abuse guardrail — "keep abuse under ~0.5%" — has no stated denominator or detection method.
3. **Bypassing inspection on 35% of volume** with 3–5% audit sampling has a materially asymmetric error cost: a misgraded unit shipped to a new customer causes a second return, a review, and possibly a lost lifetime relationship. There is no quantified cost-of-error, no category exclusion list (hygiene, intimates, food, cosmetics with expiry, electronics requiring data wipe, batteries/hazmat, safety-critical items), and no seller-of-record/counterfeit risk check. "It feels uncomfortable, which is roughly the right signal" is rhetoric, not risk analysis.
4. **Scrap is now a regulatory and reputational exposure**, not just a cost line. # Returns: A Redesign Proposal

*Draft for discussion — not a mandate. Assumptions are illustrative placeholders; swap in your actuals and the logic should hold.*

---

## 0. A note before the detail

There's a temptation in these situations to read "28% return rate" as the problem statement. I'd gently push back on that. A 28% rate in a category where customers order two sizes to keep one isn't necessarily a defect — it may be the cost of the conversion rate you're already enjoying. Customer research is telling you something worth hearing.

Three reframes seem to explain most of the leakage better than the policy does:

1. **The decision about a returned unit is currently made *after* it arrives.** That's the expensive part. Everything downstream — the queue, the double-touch, the late markdown — descends from a disposition decision that happens too late and in the wrong place.
2. **The enemy is the calendar, not the customer.** A grade-A unit is worth ~92% of ASP on day two and ~55% on day forty. Nothing physically changed. You paid for time.
3. **Return cost currently sits in operations' P&L but is created in merchandising's.** Until the buyer who chose the SKU feels the return in their number, prevention will always be someone else's project.

If those three are right, the redesign is less about restricting behaviour and more about **collapsing decision latency and relocating accountability.** What follows assumes that reading. Push back where it doesn't fit what you're seeing.

---

## 1. Where the money actually goes

Worth decomposing before prescribing. A returned unit destroys value in six places, and my suspicion is that only two of them are currently visible in anyone's reporting.

| Leak | Illustrative per returned unit | Visible today? |
|---|---|---|
| Reverse freight (prepaid label, low density) | $4.20 | Usually yes |
| Touch labour (receive, inspect, grade, repack, restock) | $2.60 | Usually yes |
| Reverse overhead (space, systems, supervision, congestion drag on outbound) | $1.40 | Rarely |
| **Value decay** (markdown taken because of elapsed time, not condition) | **$9.80** | Almost never |
| Scrap / write-off | $6.30 (blended) | Partially |
| Sunk outbound fulfilment + payment processing | $8.50 | Recognised but treated as unavoidable |

**Working illustration** (please replace): 10M units shipped, ASP $60, COGS $30, outbound fulfilment $6.50.

- Returns: 2.8M units, $168M refunded
- Blended net recovery today: ~42% of original retail (~$25.20/unit)
- Contribution on a *kept* unit: +$21.50
- Contribution on a *returned* unit: −$21.50
- **Swing per return: ~$43. Annual drag: ~$60M.** On $600M gross, that's roughly ten points of margin sitting in the reverse flow.

Notice that value decay plus scrap — the two purely self-inflicted lines — are about **$16 of the $32.80 of controllable loss.** That's where I'd look first, because it requires no change to the customer promise at all.

*Question worth putting to the finance team: does anyone currently own the value-decay line? If the answer is no, that may explain a lot.*

---

## 2. Prevention — reduce the *reason*, not the *right*

The goal isn't a lower return rate. It's a lower rate of **avoidable, low-recovery** returns, with conversion and repeat-purchase held flat or better as an explicit guardrail. Some returns are profitable to encourage; the trick is knowing which.

### 2.1 Segment the reasons first

Free-text and single-dropdown reason codes are close to useless — customers pick the first plausible option. Suggest a guided, two-step taxonomy captured at RMA initiation, then *reconciled against physical grade* so you can measure how much customers under- or over-report:

| Reason cluster | Typical share | Owner | Preventable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fit / size | 35–45% (apparel) | Merch + PDP | Highly |
| Expectation gap (colour, material, scale) | 15–20% | Content | Highly |
| Damaged in transit | 6–10% | Packaging + carrier | Highly |
| Defective / quality | 8–12% | Vendor | Highly, via chargeback |
| Wrong item / short ship | 3–5% | Fulfilment | Fully |
| Bracketing (intentional multi-buy) | 10–15% | Nobody, currently | Partly — and possibly shouldn't be |
| Remorse / no longer needed | 8–12% | — | Low |
| Abuse / wardrobing / serial | 1–3% | Risk | Yes, quietly |

### 2.2 Interventions, roughly in order of payback

**Pre-purchase**
- **Size intelligence from your own return exhaust.** You already know that customers who returned SKU-A in M kept it in L. That's a recommendation engine sitting unused. Expect 15–25% reduction in size-driven returns on covered SKUs; coverage matters more than model sophistication.
- **PDP truthfulness audits on the worst 200 SKUs by return rate.** Measured dimensions, on-body scale reference, fabric behaviour, video. Cheap, unglamorous, reliably effective.
- **Bracketing made explicit rather than accidental.** If a customer has two sizes in the cart, you have a choice: block it (loses share — the research is right), ignore it (costs $43 per returned unit), or *serve it deliberately* — offer a size advisor, or a "try both, return the spare free at a drop-off point" flow that steers the reverse leg into your cheapest, fastest lane. The third option turns a cost into a controlled cost.
- **Review surfacing weighted toward fit signal**, not star rating.

**Post-purchase, pre-return** — this is the highest-yield and most neglected window.
- **Exchange-first RMA flow.** Default to size/colour exchange with instant dispatch and a small incentive; refund available but one click deeper. Typical conversion 20–35% of eligible intents. This preserves *revenue*, not just margin — materially better than any cost reduction.
- **Returnless refund ("keep it") on a computed threshold**, not a flat rule. Approve when `expected net recovery < reverse freight + touch cost + expected decay`. On low-ASP, high-freight, low-recovery items this is simply the dominant choice. Typically 8–15% of return volume qualifies; gate it with velocity limits per customer to keep abuse under ~0.5%.
- **Partial keep / repair-kit / missing-part dispatch** for cosmetic or incomplete-order cases. Often converts a $43 loss into a $4 cost.
- **Defect containment at source.** Vendor scorecards with a returns reserve withheld per PO, released on performance. This changes supplier behaviour faster than any inspection regime.
- **Packaging redesign for the worst transit-damage SKUs.** Damage rate is a design variable, not weather.

### 2.3 Guardrails so prevention doesn't become tightening in disguise

Every prevention change ships as an experiment with three co-primary metrics: **return rate, conversion, and 12-month repeat rate of the exposed cohort.** Any intervention that improves return rate while degrading repeat rate is a loss, and should be reversed regardless of how good the operations number looks. I'd make that a standing rule and hold the team to it publicly.

---

## 3. Triage and grading — decide before it moves

The manual inspection queue is a symptom. The queue exists because disposition is decided at the dock. Move the decision upstream and most of the queue disappears.

### 3.1 Predicted disposition at RMA initiation

At the moment the customer requests a return, you know: SKU, condition self-report, guided photos, reason code, customer history, days-since-delivery, current inventory position, season position, and secondary-market price. That is more than enough to predict a disposition class with useful accuracy.

The RMA then carries a **disposition code printed on the label / encoded in the QR**, which determines routing before the unit is collected.

| Grade | Definition | Target share | Route | Net recovery target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Sellable as-new, sealed/unworn | 40–48% | Cross-dock → nearest FC forward stock | 88–96% of ASP |
| **B** | Open-box, cosmetically imperfect | 20–25% | RPC → own certified/open-box storefront | 62–78% |
| **C** | Functional, needs refurb or parts | 12–18% | RPC refurb cell or specialist partner | 45–65% post-refurb |
| **D** | Harvest / component or bulk B2B | 8–12% | Direct to jobber / auction | 10–25% |
| **E** | Recycle / regulated disposal | ≤4% | Certified processor | ~0 to negative |

### 3.2 Trusted fast lane

Grade-A prediction on a low-risk SKU from a low-risk customer should **bypass physical inspection entirely** and go direct to forward stock, with statistical audit sampling (start at 15%, decay to 3–5% as false-positive rate proves out) rather than 100% inspection. Target **35% of all returns cross-docked with zero inspection touch** by month twelve.

This is the single biggest labour and latency lever available. It also feels uncomfortable, which is roughly the right signal — the discomfort is a proxy for how much money the current caution is costing.

### 3.3 The queue rule

No unit sits "awaiting decision." Ever. A disposition is assigned within 4 hours of dock scan, or the system auto-assigns the default for that SKU class. **WIP age distribution becomes a daily-reviewed metric**, and any unit older than 72 hours triggers automatic escalation down the channel waterfall. Ambiguity is fine at the edges; ambiguity in the middle of a decaying-asset queue is expensive.

**SLA targets:** dock-to-disposition ≤ 4h · dock-to-resale-live ≤ 48h for A/B · refund issued at first carrier scan, not at receipt (this is a customer-promise upgrade that costs almost nothing and buys goodwill for everything else).

---

## 4. Refurbishment and secondary channels

### 4.1 Refurb only where the arithmetic says so

A simple gate, applied per SKU-grade pair and recalculated weekly:

> **Refurbish if:** `(price at grade N+1 − price at grade N) > refurb cost × (1 + rework failure rate) + handling delay decay`

Four tiers, ascending cost:
1. **Clean / repack / reseal** — $1.20–2.50. Almost always positive. Highest-volume activity by far.
2. **Accessory or consumable replacement from a parts bank** built from grade-D harvest — $3–8. Often the best-return activity in the whole operation, because the input is free.
3. **Technical repair** — $12–40. In-house only for high-velocity categories; otherwise a specialist partner on a per-unit or revenue-share basis.
4. **Harvest** — recover components to feed tier 2, then recycle the shell.

Make/buy: I'd resist building technical rep
